title: Lav 1
hook: the first round: take up the work of dharma and the Name (Suhi M4, ang 773)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Friend came to the house, and your line: the friend is home. Did you welcome someone through your door, or back into your day? Today the friend stays, because today a wedding begins. Day six hundred sixty-two.

It's early morning at a gurdwara, and the hall is full of bright clothes. The bride and groom sit side by side on the floor, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, with a long scarf joining them, his end on his shoulder, hers in her hand. The hall goes quiet as the granthi turns to the page. The couple doesn't write vows. The words that marry them are a Guru's, and they come in four rounds. Today, the first: lav one.
screen: `A MORNING WEDDING IN A GURDWARA.` → `NO VOWS OF THEIR OWN.` → `FOUR ROUNDS OF WORDS.`

segments.voice: The Sikh wedding is called the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. At its center are four stanzas by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, in Raag Suhi, on Ang seven seventy-three. Each stanza is a lav, a round, and together they're the laavan. The pattern is simple. The granthi reads the first stanza aloud. Then the ragis sing it, and while they sing, the couple stands and walks once around the Guru Granth Sahib, clockwise, the groom usually a step ahead, the bride holding her end of the scarf. They bow, sit, and the next stanza is read. Four readings, four songs, four walks. What does the first round say? In paraphrase: in the first round, the Lord sets out the work of the householder's life. Take the Guru's word as your scripture; hold to dharma, right living; remember the Name. Notice what's missing. The first lav doesn't talk about romance, or the families, or the future house. It talks about a way of life the two will now walk together. Sikh teachers often read the four rounds on two levels at once: a husband and wife beginning a shared life, and a soul beginning its journey toward God. Round one is where both journeys start: with ordinary duty, done with the Name in mind. Guru Ram Das wrote it as a householder himself, a married man with children. In Sikh teaching that matters: the spiritual life isn't found by running away from home, but walked right through it.
screen: `ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.` · `READ, THEN SUNG, THEN WALKED.` · `ROUND ONE: DUTY, THE WORD, THE NAME.` · `TWO JOURNEYS IN ONE WALK.` · then, large: `ROUND ONE: DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one slow circle. If you have room, stand and walk a small circle, around a chair, a table, or just a spot on the floor, clockwise, slowly, one full round. If you can't walk, trace a circle with your hand. As you go, think of one plain duty in your life, the dishes, a shift at work, a call to a parent, and let it be part of the circle, not an interruption to it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you finish the round. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Lav. A round: one of the four stanzas of the Sikh wedding, read, sung, and walked around the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: round one: dharma. Today, do one ordinary duty as if it were part of a ceremony, slowly and on purpose. Day six hundred sixty-two.
